library(tidyverse)

## Problem 1

### Birthday simulation

```{r}
# Function to determine whether a group has at least
# two people sharing the same birthday
birthday_sim = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

# Simulate the birthday problem 10,000 times
# for group sizes from 2 to 50
set.seed(123)

birthday_results = tibble(
  group_size = 2:50
) |>
  mutate(
    simulations = map(
      group_size,
      ~ replicate(10000, birthday_sim(.x))
    ),
    probability = map_dbl(
      simulations,
      mean
    )
  )

# Plot estimated probabilities
ggplot(birthday_results,
       aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated Probability of Shared Birthdays",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Estimated Probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Interpretation

The estimated probability of at least two people sharing a birthday increases as the group size increases. This occurs because larger groups have more possible pairs of individuals, increasing the chance of a shared birthday. The probability reaches approximately 50% with a group of 23 people and continues increasing as the group size grows.

## Problem 2

### Import and tidy the data

```{r}

# Get the names of all CSV files
file_names =
  list.files(
    path = "data/data",
    pattern = "\\.csv$",
    full.names = TRUE
  )

# Create a dataframe containing filenames and imported data
study_data =
  tibble(
    file_name = file_names,
    arm = if_else(str_detect(file_names, "con"), "control", "experimental"),
    subject_id = str_extract(basename(file_names), "\\d+"),
    data = map(file_names, read_csv)
  )

# Combine all observations and reshape into tidy format
study_tidy =
  study_data |>
  unnest(data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = factor(week, levels = paste0("week_", 1:8))
  )

# Display the tidy dataset
study_tidy
```


### Spaghetti plot

```{r}

study_tidy |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = interaction(arm, subject_id),
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Observations Over Time by Study Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Study Arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The spaghetti plot suggests that observations in the experimental group generally increase over time, whereas the control group tends to remain at lower levels. Although there is variability among individual participants in both groups, the experimental group shows a more pronounced upward trend, suggesting a potential difference in outcomes between the two study arms.

# Problem 3

## Simulation

```{r}
set.seed(123)

n = 30
sigma = 5
n_sim = 5000

mu_values = 0:6

simulate_data = function(mu) {
  x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

  broom::tidy(t.test(x, mu = 0)) |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

simulation_results =
  expand_grid(
    mu = mu_values,
    simulation = 1:n_sim
  ) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(mu, simulate_data)
  ) |>
  unnest(results)
```


```{r}
#Calculate power and average estimates

simulation_summary = simulation_results %>%
  mutate(reject_null = p.value < 0.05) %>%
  group_by(mu) %>%
  summarize(
    power = mean(reject_null),
    average_estimate = mean(estimate),
    average_estimate_rejected = if (any(reject_null)) {
      mean(estimate[reject_null])
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  )

simulation_summary


#Plot power versus true mean

simulation_summary %>%
  filter(mu > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Power vs. True Mean",
    x = "True Mean",
    y = "Power"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


#Plot average estimates versus true mean

simulation_summary %>%
  filter(mu > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mu)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = average_estimate, color = "All simulations")
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = average_estimate, color = "All simulations")
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = average_estimate_rejected, color = "Rejected null")
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = average_estimate_rejected, color = "Rejected null")
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimates vs. True Mean",
    x = "True Mean",
    y = "Average Estimated Mean",
    color = "Estimate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The estimated power increases as the true population mean increases. When the true mean is close to zero, the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis is relatively low. As the true mean increases, the test becomes more likely to detect a statistically significant difference.

The average estimated mean across all simulations is close to the true population mean, indicating that the sample mean is approximately unbiased. However, among simulations where the null hypothesis is rejected, the average estimates tend to be higher than the true mean, particularly for smaller effect sizes. This occurs because selecting only statistically significant results introduces selection bias.
